marble.name: Phases of the Moon
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Explain the phases of the Moon as the changing angle of sunlight on the lunar surface as seen from Earth, and describe how solar and lunar eclipses occur
marble.prompt: If you noticed the Moon looking like a thin crescent one night and a full circle two weeks later, could they explain what has changed and why — and describe what happens during a lunar eclipse?

cluster.summary: Your child is discovering how daylight changes throughout the year by observing that days are longer in summer and shorter in winter.

misconceptions: Phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon (the dominant misconception; actually that is a lunar eclipse, which is rare)
Phases are caused by clouds, or by planets/other bodies blocking the Moon
The Moon is only present in the sky at night, or the far side is permanently dark ('dark side of the Moon')
A solar and a lunar eclipse are the same event, or an eclipse happens every month (fails to account for the Moon's tilted orbit)
The Moon does not rotate / the phase is a fixed property of the Moon rather than of the viewing geometry
representations: Sun-Earth-Moon orbital diagram showing the Moon always half-lit, with eight positions round the orbit and the matching Earth-view phase drawn beside each
The ball-and-lamp physical model (child's head = Earth, ball = Moon, single bright lamp = Sun)
Phase strip / circular sequence: new → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent
Eclipse alignment diagram distinguishing umbra/penumbra and the straight-line Sun-Moon-Earth (solar) vs Sun-Earth-Moon (lunar) arrangements
authoredAnswer: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon; phases are how much of that lit half we can SEE from Earth as the Moon orbits us — set by the changing angle between Sun, Earth and Moon. The dark part of a crescent is the Moon's own unlit side, not the Earth's shadow. The Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which is rare.
probe: In a darkened room use a single bright lamp as the Sun and give the child a ball on a stick as the Moon, with their own head as the Earth. Ask them to PREDICT with a reason: as you slowly turn the ball around your head, will it go through crescent → half → full, and what makes the dark part? Many predict their own head

wrongAnswers.wrong: The dark part is the Earth's shadow cast onto the Moon.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: attributes the dark part of the Moon to the Earth's shadow
wrongAnswers.fix: Couple an orbit-view with a sky-view and park at full Moon: the Earth's shadow points AWAY into space; the dark part is the Moon's own unlit side seen at an angle.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: talks about the Moon's own light being blocked or the Moon dimming itself
wrongAnswers.fix: The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight and half is always lit; phases are about our viewing angle, not the Moon changing its own light.

wrongAnswers.wrong: A crescent Moon is a partial eclipse.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: calls a crescent a 'partial eclipse,' or says an eclipse should happen every month
wrongAnswers.fix: Phases happen monthly (viewing angle); eclipses are rare alignments where a shadow really is cast, rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's.
